opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the uncertainty is huge, and I want to be upfront about that. The way I think about it is that a scenario isn't a prediction in the sense of "this is exactly what will happen." It's more like one concrete trajectory drawn from the distribution of what I think could happen, ideally from somewhere near the middle of that distribution, near my median.

The reason to write it out concretely, instead of just saying "I think AGI is probably coming around such-and-such a year with wide error bars," is that concreteness forces you to confront things you'd otherwise gloss over. When you say "AI gets really powerful and then things get crazy," that hides a lot. But when you have to write: okay, in this month, this company has this many copies of this model running at this speed, and here's what the government knows, and here's what China does in response, you hit all these questions you hadn't thought about. Sometimes you realize your abstract views don't fit together. That's really valuable.

So the process was roughly: we started from our quantitative models, things like compute forecasts, trends in benchmarks, our estimates of how much AI research automation speeds up progress. Then we wrote it period by period. Write what happens in the first chunk, then the next, and so on, trying to make each step the most plausible continuation given what came before, instead of working backwards from a dramatic ending. We ran tabletop exercises and wargames with people playing the companies, governments, the AIs themselves, to stress-test how actors would actually behave. And we got a lot of feedback from experts who would say "no, that's not how this would go," and we'd revise.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that we deliberately wrote branches. There's the "race" ending and the "slowdown" ending, because the point where things diverge is actually a decision point, and we wanted to show that the outcome isn't fixed. The future depends on choices people make.

And I'd say to people: please don't anchor too hard on the specific dates. Things could easily go slower than we depict, and some of my coauthors have longer timelines than the scenario itself. What I hope people take away is less "this will happen in 2027" and more "here's what it might actually look like, concretely, and here are the dynamics we should be watching for." If someone thinks it's wrong, great. I'd love for them to write their own scenario showing how they think it goes, because that's how we get a better collective picture.

r001.rationale: The response says they wrote the scenario period by period, making each step the most plausible continuation given what came before.

r002.rationale: It says they deliberately wrote race and slowdown branches to show the outcome is not fixed and depends on people’s choices, and cautions readers not to anchor too hard on the specific dates.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the first thing to say is that I don't think the scenario is going to happen. Like, if you asked me "what's the probability that things unfold the way AI 2027 describes," it's very low, because any specific detailed story about the future is going to be wrong in lots of ways. That's just the nature of the exercise.

But I think that's actually fine, and it's kind of the point. The way I think about it is: there are a bunch of different levels at which you can be uncertain. You can be uncertain about the timelines — when do we get to AIs that can automate AI research? You can be uncertain about takeoff speeds — once you get there, how fast does it go from there to superintelligence? You can be uncertain about alignment — do the AIs end up with the goals we intended or not? And then there's all the geopolitics on top of that: what does the US government do, what does China do, how do the companies behave.

What we tried to do is, for each of those, pick what we thought was our best guess, or at least a reasonably likely branch, and then follow the implications through concretely. And the value of doing it concretely, rather than just saying "I think there's a 30% chance of X by 2030," is that when you actually have to write down what happens month by month, you notice things. You notice that two of your beliefs are in tension, or that some step you were hand-waving over actually requires something you hadn't thought about. We had a lot of those moments. The timelines and takeoff models we published alongside the scenario came out of exactly that process — we'd write a paragraph, realise we didn't actually know how fast something would happen, and go build a model to figure out what we believed.

The other thing is that I had done this once before. Back in 2021 I wrote "What 2026 Looks Like," and that was the same kind of exercise, and it held up — not perfectly, but a lot better than I expected. And that gave me some confidence that even though any given detail is probably wrong, the shape of the thing can be informative, and it's worth putting your neck out.

So when people say "how can you write this if you're so uncertain?" my answer is basically: the uncertainty is why you should write it. If I were certain, I'd just tell you the answer. Since I'm not, the most useful thing I can do is show you one fleshed-out path through the possibility space, be explicit that it's one path and not a prediction, and let people argue with the specific steps. That's much more productive than arguing about vague abstractions. We even wrote two different endings — the slowdown ending and the race ending — partly to make the point that this branches, and that the branch point matters enormously.

And then I try to be honest about where my own views have shifted since. My median timelines have actually gotten a bit longer since we published, so if I were writing it today I'd probably call it AI 2028 or something. I'd rather say that publicly than pretend the scenario is a fixed prophecy.

r001.rationale: The response says the authors chose their best guesses for several uncertainties and followed the implications month by month, but does not clearly say they repeatedly chose the most plausible continuation given the events already depicted.

r002.rationale: The response says the scenario is one path, not a prediction, and describes two endings to show that the future branches. This communicates that readers should not treat the single scenario as definitive.

astra-6.text:
I think of a scenario like AI 2027 as a way of making uncertainty concrete, rather than making it go away. If you just say, “AI could become very powerful quite soon,” it’s easy to nod along without really thinking through what that would involve. Writing a scenario forces you to ask: what happens first? What capabilities would be needed for the next step? How would people respond?

Of course, every time you fill in one of those details, you could be wrong. So I wouldn’t want someone to read it as a claim that this exact sequence of events will happen. The point is to lay out a plausible trajectory in enough detail that we can examine the assumptions and disagree about particular steps.

There’s a tension there, because a vivid narrative can feel much more certain than it actually is. You have to keep distinguishing between the story you’re telling and your confidence in its individual parts. You might think a broad development is fairly likely while being very uncertain about its timing or which organisation gets there first.

Ideally, the scenario becomes a starting point for asking, “What would have to be different for things to go another way?” And as new evidence comes in, you revise it. The value is in making your picture of the future explicit enough that you can learn where it’s wrong.

r001.rationale: The response calls the scenario a plausible trajectory and says its assumptions can be examined, but does not describe choosing the most plausible continuation at each stage.

r002.rationale: It cautions that the scenario is not an exact prediction and invites considering how things could go differently, but does not explain that depicting multiple futures prevents overreliance on one scenario.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of a scenario as a way of making your uncertainty concrete. You take a bunch of things that seem plausible individually and ask, “Can I put these together into a coherent story? And when I do, what implications emerge that I hadn’t noticed before?”

The danger is that a detailed story can sound much more certain than you actually are. I don’t think the future is going to unfold exactly as described in AI 2027. There are lots of points where things could go differently, including the timing. The useful question is whether the story captures important dynamics, and which assumptions those dynamics depend on.

So my approach is to write something specific enough that people can disagree with it. If someone says, “This step seems implausible,” we can ask why, consider an alternative, and see how much of the rest of the scenario changes. That’s much more useful than just saying, “AI could have a huge impact, but there’s a lot of uncertainty.”

r001.rationale: The response describes combining plausible elements into a coherent story, but does not say it was built stage by stage by choosing the most plausible continuation given preceding events.

r002.rationale: It says the future may unfold differently and discusses assumptions, but does not explain that depicting multiple possible futures is meant to keep readers from overweighting one scenario.
